posts.text:
I guess what I've seen from Chinese laser capacity expansion: 

1. Dongshan/Source Photonics (索尔思): 9M/month capacity -> 22M/month Q4 ->  300m/year in 2027 (mostly EML, but blended)

Claims of 1B/year "target" for laser chips with no deadline, but I'd take this as a grain of salt. 

2. Shijia (仕佳): 72M/year for 100mW CW, 2-3 year project (mainly 2029 full capacity online)

3. Yunling (云岭): 18.75M/year 70/100mW CW, 3 year schedule (mainly 2029 full capacity online)

4. Ligent (纳真), some reports stated 170M target for total capacity (also blended, lot of which is 200G EML)

5. Yuanjie: ~10M/year currently, expanding for early 2027 and 2028, but no quantities. 

6. Hongchen: I think this was the perfect example of flooding H2 2026 arguments. With some some optical bears claiming 60-70M capacity...

But this turned out to completely wrong... Their actual statements were "70/100 mW products are entering small-volume production". 

7. Dingxin Optoelectronics - Targeting 15M/year blended (with 70/100mW CW and 100G EML lines)

Obviously mapped many others like Everbright/Accelink and did some guesses around laser mixes, but only included public disclosures. 

From your pluggable vendor channel checks: 

- 70mW/100mW lasers are actually a bottleneck right now per Innolight/Cambridge channel checks, laser ASPs actually increasing. 

Lasers are tighter than they were a few months ago. 

I don't think there's a giant moat here, Chinese players are already competitive. But a bottleneck is a bottleneck, and anyone with capacity to monetize that will benefit, since it's a volume game. 

In terms of what the larger pluggable makers are actually doing: 

- Innolight September disclosure: actively introducing new suppliers and are planning to sign 2-3 year-long contracts to lock upstream capacity for lasers (still actively securing supply for 1.6T pluggables)

So there's some game theory over who can lock up qualified capacity among all your players. 

Even if there's some over-ordering, laser BOM is cheap, so they'd probably want to lock up capacity with more suppliers than lose billions in downstream revenue. (also kinda hurts competitors) 

- High end lines (for CPO), non-competitive with Western players like $LITE / $COHR as of next few years. But Chinese players would eventually develop the technology. 

- $AAOI CEO: Chinese suppliers several years behind on high-power CPO/DWDM laser production "not in the next 2,3 years"

- $LITE CEO questioned whether claimed Chinese manufacturing capacity was translating into commercial output. "At least at the moment, we see no impact from any Chinese laser supply."

This is despite Shijia, Everbright, Yuanjie and others stating 400mW capabilities and capacity expansion targets from Chinese companies. Although Western CEOs might be disputing their reliability and capability to scale these lines. 

I see lower end range bottleneck for pluggable will gradually ease as more capacity comes online 2028. But all evidence points against near-term overflooding. 

The 100mW range for example, someone cited 2 years of equipment investment. Higher ranges were 3 years for equipment investment? So even some Chinese players take years for capacity to come online. 

The multi year laser shortage statements from laser company executives seems to be true... especially among higher end ranges, since buildout takes a lot of time. 

Legitimate competition coming from China, but as of now there's a scramble for CW LTAs among the industry in 2026-2027. 

Lot of capacity is probably allocated toward higher spec lasers or EML, as seen with EML bottlenecking $LITE for the longest time (they have more supply now) that they had to buy CW off the market instead of supplying it themselves. 

This is while tail end for 800G demand for example, might continue much much longer than expected with sovereign DC buildouts. So there might be some surprising dynamics for duration, we'll see.

In the end I do think supply chains will be bif

posts.name: S.E. Robinson, Jr.
posts.text:
THE BORING COMPANY HQ: Bastrop, Texas, October

Here is my flyover of TBC's Bastrop headquarters and Prufrock factory. It's is where they test every machine before it ships, build and store equipment, precast tunnel segments, liner trucks, vertical cassettes and conveyor belt systems, and more. They house their Prufrock Command Center here to control all the Prufrock's soon to be around the world.

- The SpaceX Pedestrian Tunnel started as Porpoise Test 6 (PT6). TBC first bored it to test (no people in the tunnel) ZPIT continuous mining, an upgraded liner truck and the "SNAILS on RAILS" navigation system. After the test, they turned it into a 500 ft walkway under FM1209 that connects the SpaceX site to Hyperloop Plaza, where The Boring Bodega is. People use it so they don't have to cross that busy road on foot.
 
- Hard-rock Prufrock-MB4 being constructed for Nashville's Music City LOOP.

- The Test Tunnel PT5 connects SpaceX's Starlink factory to TBC under FM1209. It was the first use of custom hexagonal segments, automated gantry steering, quick craneless retrieval, and the first version of ZPIT. It's now a test bench for liner trucks, vertical cassettes and new belt systems.

- Hyperloop Test Tunnel was PT4; the first craneless, pitless retrieval of the machine. It's now a vacuum tunnel for Hyperloop vacuum pump system testing. It also connects SpaceX's Starlink factory to TBC under FM1209.

- Lastly, Prufrock-5 after completing a test tunnel connecting Ring Ranch and possibly the SpaceX Starmind Factory. I videoed it right before it was loaded up and shipped to San Antonio, Texas, for the Morgan's Wonderland Tunnel.

If you have any questions, leave them in the comments. Subscriber Photo-thread and Support links in the thread.

Thanks for watching!

posts.text:
In early 2002, Elon was preparing to launch SpaceX and searching for the people who could help him build a rocket from scratch. One Sunday in January 2002, he walked into a friend's rented warehouse in Huntington Beach and found Tom Mueller holding an 80-pound rocket engine on his shoulder, trying to bolt it to a frame. It was the largest liquid-fuel engine any amateur had ever built, with 13,000 pounds of thrust, made in Tom's spare time. 

Elon asked the main question  “Could you build something bigger?”

The next Sunday Elon came to his house. It was Super Bowl Sunday; they watched maybe one play, because they were too busy sketching the first SpaceX rocket.

Tom became SpaceX employee #1, and the man who built engines on weekends went on to build Merlin, Kestrel and Draco. 

Elon saw a person, not a résumé, someone who built rockets with his own hands simply because he loved them.

posts.name: The All-In Podcast
posts.text:
David Friedberg: France’s Crisis Is a Warning for America

“France is a bellwether for the West.

So take a look at this chart. This chart is a measure of public spending as a percent of GDP.

And you can see the comparison of France's public spending as a % of GDP to the peak public spending as a % of GDP of major communist nations.”

@Chamath:

“So do you think France is a communist state? They spend like it.”

@Jason:

“Well, it's certainly been a socialist state, right?”

Chamath:

“Is it working?”

@Friedberg:

“That's my point. And I think this is such a prescient lesson for the West to look at.

We all think that there's some political problem with Macron or whoever it was.

The more the government spends, the worse the conditions get for its people, not the opposite, and then the people riot and revolt.

Take a guess where the US is today. US public spending is roughly 36% of GDP. France today is operating its national government spending deficit is 5.4% of GDP. The US is actually 6.2% of GDP.

France is, I think, probably the first to go because they're only growing their economy at half a percent while the US is growing at 2.3%.

So we're still kind of hanging on because we have some degree of economic growth that's allowing us to kind of hold things together.

But I would argue that we are facing the same sort of fiscal cliff which leads to this extraordinary social unrest as France.

All the economic measures are aligned, we're at the same rate, we're at the same set of problems, and we're starting to see the cracks in the system.

There's probably a multi-year solution.”

The French bond spread, now at 1.69 percentage points, is rapidly approaching the peak reached at the height of the Eurozone debt crisis.

So, are we in a crisis? Will France default?

The answer to the second question is no, assuming the ECB prints money and cuts interest rates when things get really ugly.

Are we in a crisis? Well, that depends.

Not the kind of turmoil we witnessed during the Eurozone debt crisis, when it was unclear whether Greece and Italy could remain in the eurozone.

Many years and countless ECB bond-buying programs later, we know governments and central banks will work together to keep things from falling apart.

Yet I would call this a bond crisis.

Because after nearly six years of negative nominal returns (and an even worse picture after inflation), we now have another painful reminder that bonds are no longer the asset class they once were.

Not only have bonds delivered negative returns, but their risk profile has also deteriorated significantly, while their diversification benefits have largely evaporated.

Bond returns have become positively correlated with equity returns. And I expect that relationship to persist for one simple reason: bonds themselves have become a risky asset.

To be clear, at current yields, bonds could certainly deliver positive returns once interest rates decline.

But that doesn't mean bonds will magically return to being a low-risk asset class offering decent positive returns and meaningful diversification.

Quite the

posts.name: Byrne Hobart
posts.text:
This is not a very good point, and it doesn't advance the discussion at all. There is an enormous burden of proof on you to argue that giving additional dollars to California is net beneficial, whereas the equity and bond markets' willingness to finance an expensive AI buildout provides ample evidence that people who know what they're talking about believe that dollars in the hands of these tech executives will produce something of value. Maybe you're smarter than all of them, but the way you advocate this wealth tax implies that you're going to great lengths to disguise this.

Further, your point about the cyclicality of this tax revenue accidentally raises another point that is very damaging to your campaign. California's tax system is already cyclical! They're already overreliant on a small number of taxpayers compared to other states (different ones each year, but for CA to work it really needs to be the place where successful tech executives want to realize liquidity). The top 1% paid half the state's income taxes in 2021—then 40% less a year later, because tech stocks went down.

A one-time wealth tax theoretically avoids this, because you just levy it when assets are expensive. But as far as I can tell, the plan is to spend the money in five years and hope somebody else has solve the state's budget problems by then. This is not what people conventionally refer to as a "plan." So I take Zucman at his word (iffy proposition!) when he says he wants it to be a regular thing. 

If we're going to tax a form of wealth, I have an idea should really tickle you as an economist, or at least as a guy who probably hangs out with them from time to time: tax the land! It's a broader tax base, land values are far more stable than equity, and land, of course, cannot hop on its private jet and head to Miami. This also has a salutary effect on California politics, by sending every homeowner in the state a shocking bill from time to time. This will get voters asking themselves the same question you refuse to answer: what good is the state doing with all of that money?

I still find it puzzling that you're making such unsophisticated arguments, here. Surely, you can do better, and can explain what it is that the government California will do with another few billion dollars that it hasn't accomplished with the first $350bn or so.

As I've shown you a few times now, it's entirely possible to have a well-informed, reasonable argument about the proposed wealth tax. All you have to do is switch sides.

posts.name: Blake Madden 🏥
posts.text:
A new coalition, the Association for Direct Care, has launched with a mix of health systems, physician advocacy, and employer-purchaser muscle behind it.

The mission is to get more employers and clinicians dealing directly with each other, cut out the administrative bloat, and bring some transparency to how care gets purchased.

Alyssa Simpson Rochwerger, co-founder and CEO of Grounded Health @getgroundedhlth, which joined the coalition, explained, “Every other dollar a company spends is visible. Finance can see software spend, travel spend, payroll — down to the transaction. Healthcare is the one place where an employer pays the bill and never sees the receipt.”

Direct contracting is being pitched as the fix: real access to claims and pricing data, less middleman, more accountability.

What they're actually asking for:

• Expanding direct contracting across commercial markets and federal health programs
• Better access to healthcare data
• Fewer regulatory/administrative barriers standing between patients, employers, and providers

I have to wonder how much traction this gets with Congress in the near term, but the timing tracks. Indiana's already built laws specifically enabling direct-to-employer arrangements, and groups like this tend to be a signal that a policy push is coming, not just a press release. 

Worth keeping an eye on who else joins in the coming months.

Press release: https://employerdirectcare.org/association-for-direct-care-launches-to-lower-health-care-costs-and-expand-direct-contracting/
Learn more: https://employerdirectcare.org/
